content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.85.

**How I set it up:** I trained the learner on just one task, L1-S1-M1. Then I tested tasks chosen so that the two hypotheses predict different results. Some tasks had few new rules but looked very different from the trained task. Others had more new rules but were fairly similar to it.

| Test task | New rules | Similarity to trained task | Mean examples needed (tests) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M1 (the trained task) | 0 | 1.0 | ~15 (3) |
| L1-S1-M4 | 1 | 0.75 | ~15 (5) |
| L3-S1-M1, L1-S1-M2 | 1 | 0 | ~23 (16) |
| L1-S2-M4 | 2 | 0.56 | ~35 (5) |
| L4-S2-M4 | 3 | 0.56 | ~39 (6) |

**Why part-based:** The cost went up with the number of new rules. The tasks with zero similarity were clearly easier than the ones with 0.56 similarity, which is the opposite of what a holistic learner would show.

**Why not higher confidence:** Single tests were very noisy; one zero-similarity task ranged from 6 to 53 examples. The main gap (about 23 vs about 36 examples) is roughly 2.5–3 standard errors. The step from 2 to 3 new rules (35 vs 39) is small and could be noise.

I used 36 of the 60 budget units (1 training, 35 tests).
